9150:
To interweave means to weave two or more things together so that they cross through and over each other, becoming tightly connected — almost inseparable — as a single, unified whole.

The key image to hold in your mind is a piece of woven fabric. In fabric, horizontal threads cross over and under vertical threads, back and forth, again and again. No single thread just sits next to another — each thread passes through the others. That crossing, locking pattern is what "interweave" captures. The individual threads are still there, but together they form something much larger and stronger.

In its most direct, physical sense, to interweave means to literally weave things together — threads, strips, branches, ribbons, reeds, or any flexible material.

For example:

  • A basket-maker interweaves thin strips of wood to create a basket.
  • A craft artist interweaves ribbons of different colors to make a decorative braid.
  • Vines in a forest can interweave as they grow, forming a thick, tangled canopy.

In each case, the materials don't just touch — they pass through each other in an alternating, crossing pattern.

This is where the word truly comes alive, and where you'll encounter it most often.

When used figuratively, interweave means to combine abstract things — ideas, stories, emotions, themes, events, cultures — so closely and deeply that they become part of one another. They don't just exist alongside each other; they cross through each other, the way threads do in cloth.

Here are some clear examples:

  • A novelist might interweave two separate storylines throughout a book — jumping from one story to the other and back, so that the two plots feel connected and support each other, rather than being completely separate.
  • A great speech might interweave humor and sadness — the two emotions don't come in separate, isolated blocks; they blend through each other so that you're laughing and feeling moved at the same time.
  • Music composers often interweave multiple melodies — each melody weaves through the others, so you can hear them individually but they also sound like one unified piece.
  • Historians say that the histories of two neighboring countries are deeply interwoven — meaning the events of one country are so tangled up with those of the other that you cannot fully understand one without the other.

What makes "interweave" different from simpler words like mix or combine is the sense of deep, structural connection.

When things are interwoven:

1. They cross through each other, not just sit next to each other.
Two colors of paint that are mixed blend and disappear into each other. But two colors of thread that are interwoven stay distinct — you can still see each color — yet they are locked together in a crossing structure. Interweave preserves the identity of the individual parts while joining them tightly.

2. They support and depend on each other.
In woven fabric, each thread holds the others in place. Pull one thread out and the fabric weakens or falls apart. When ideas, stories, or themes are interwoven, they similarly hold each other up. Remove one, and the whole feels incomplete.

3. Separating them is hard.
Things that have been interwoven are not easy to pull apart. This is a strong, structural kind of blending — not a loose or casual mixing.

Since you want a complete picture, here are the different forms of the verb:

  • To interweave — the base/infinitive form. ("They decided to interweave the two melodies.")
  • Interweaves — third person singular, present tense. ("She interweaves personal stories into her lectures.")
  • Interweaving — present participle, used for ongoing action. ("He is interweaving several themes in his novel.")
  • Interwove — simple past tense. ("The director interwove the two storylines beautifully.")
  • Interwoven — past participle, used with "have/has/had" or as an adjective. ("The themes are interwoven throughout the poem." / "The two cultures have long been interwoven.")

Note that interwoven is especially useful and common as an adjective — you'll often see it used to describe something that has already been woven together: "Their lives were deeply interwoven."

Knowing related words will sharpen your understanding of exactly what "interweave" means.

Intertwine — very close in meaning. Intertwine suggests things twisting around each other (think of two vines spiraling around each other). Interweave specifically evokes the over-and-under, crossing pattern of weaving. In practice, people use these almost interchangeably.

Interlace — nearly identical to interweave. It emphasizes a lacing or crossing pattern, like shoelaces. Very similar feel.

Blend — to mix things together smoothly until distinctions are reduced. Blend feels more like stirring; interweave feels more like structured crossing.

Merge — to combine things so that they lose their separate identities and become one thing. When things merge, the individual parts disappear. When things interweave, the individual parts are still somewhat identifiable — the threads are still visible in the cloth.

Knit — to join or connect closely. Used figuratively ("a tightly knit community"), but without the visual sense of crossing threads that interweave carries.

These are words that mean the opposite:

  • Separate — to pull apart or keep apart.
  • Disentangle — to undo something that has become tangled or interwoven.
  • Unravel — to undo a woven or tangled structure, thread by thread.
  • Isolate — to keep something alone, away from everything else.

Think of "interweave" as a word that always carries the image of a loom — of threads crossing over and under each other in a deliberate, structured pattern, creating something unified and strong. Whether you're talking about actual threads, or stories, or ideas, or cultures, or emotions — to interweave them is to bring them together in a crossing, locking, mutually-supporting way, so that the result is more than the sum of its parts, and pulling them apart would damage the whole.
9151:
Intestate is a legal adjective that describes a person who has died without leaving a valid will.

That's the heart of it. If someone dies and either never wrote a will, or wrote one that the law later rejected as invalid, that person is said to have died intestate.
Understanding It Fully: What Is a Will, and Why Does It Matter?

To truly understand "intestate," you need to understand what a will is and why it exists.

A will (sometimes called a "last will and testament") is a legal document that a person prepares while they are alive. In it, they write down exactly what they want to happen to their belongings — their money, house, car, jewellery, savings, and other possessions — after they die. They can also name who will take care of their children, and who will be responsible for carrying out their wishes.

A will gives a person control over what happens after their death.

Now, when a person dies intestate — that is, without a valid will — that control is taken away from them entirely, because they never expressed their wishes in a legally recognised way. The big question then becomes: who gets their stuff?
What Happens When Someone Dies Intestate?

This is where the law steps in. Every country, and often every region or state within a country, has a set of laws called intestacy laws (or laws of intestate succession). These are essentially the government's pre-written plan for distributing a dead person's property when that person left no instructions of their own.

These laws decide everything: who inherits the property, how much each person gets, and in what order people are considered.

The key thing to understand is this: the law does not care about your personal relationships or your private wishes. It follows a fixed, rigid formula. So even if you wanted your best friend to get your car, if you died intestate, the law would likely give that car to a blood relative instead — simply because that's what the formula says.
The Typical Order of Inheritance Under Intestacy Laws

While exact rules differ by country and jurisdiction, intestacy laws almost universally follow a hierarchy based on close family relationships. A general version of this hierarchy looks like this:

  1. Spouse / civil partner — usually the first in line, often inheriting a large share or everything
  2. Children — if there is no spouse, or sometimes alongside the spouse, children inherit
  3. Parents — if there is no spouse or children
  4. Siblings — if there are no parents
  5. More distant relatives (grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins) — considered further down the line
  6. The government — if absolutely no living relatives can be found, the deceased person's entire estate (all their property and assets) is taken by the state. This is called escheat.

Notice what's completely missing from this list: friends, unmarried long-term partners, charities, colleagues, neighbours. No matter how close these people were to the deceased in real life, intestacy laws will not automatically give them anything. Only legally recognised family relationships count.

Yes — and this is an important nuance. A person doesn't have to die entirely without a will to be intestate in some respects. If someone wrote a will but that will only covers some of their assets and leaves others unmentioned, then they are intestate with respect to those uncovered assets. The intestacy laws then kick in just for the portion the will didn't address. This is called partial intestacy.
Can a Will Be Rejected, Making Someone Intestate Even If They Wrote One?

Absolutely. Writing a will is not enough on its own — the will must also be legally valid. A will can be rejected (declared invalid) by a court for several reasons, such as:

  • It wasn't signed or witnessed properly according to the law
  • The person who wrote it was not of sound mind at the time
  • There is evidence they were pressured or manipulated into writing it
  • It was forged

If a court throws out a will for any of these reasons, the deceased is treated exactly as if they had never written one at all — they are considered intestate, and the intestacy laws take over.
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

The adjective "intestate" is used in two main ways:

Predicatively (after a verb, describing the subject):

  • "She died intestate, leaving her family to sort out the mess in court."
  • "He died intestate, so the state inherited his entire fortune."

Attributively (placed directly before a noun, modifying it):

  • "The intestate estate was divided among his three siblings."
  • "Intestate succession laws vary widely from one country to another."
  • "The court had to apply intestate distribution rules since no will existed."

When you want to refer to the condition or situation of dying without a will, the noun form is intestacy.

  • "The family was caught in a legal dispute due to the intestacy of their late father."
  • "Intestacy can cause enormous stress and conflict among surviving family members."
Why It Matters in Real Life

Dying intestate can cause serious, sometimes devastating problems for the people left behind:

  • Unintended people inherit. A distant relative you barely knew might legally receive your property while your closest friend gets nothing.
  • Unmarried partners are often left out entirely. In many countries, a partner you lived with for decades but never legally married has no automatic right to inherit anything if you die intestate. The law simply does not recognise the relationship.
  • It takes longer and costs more. Sorting out an intestate estate through the courts is typically slower, more complicated, and more expensive than carrying out the clear instructions of a valid will.
  • Family conflict. Without a clear document expressing the deceased's wishes, arguments among surviving family members are far more likely.
Intestate describes a person who has died without leaving a legally valid will, meaning the law — not the person — decides who gets everything they owned.
9152:
Intimacy is the state of being deeply close to someone — not just physically, but in a way that goes far beneath the surface. It is the feeling of being truly known by another person, and truly knowing them in return.

Think of it this way: you can stand next to a stranger in an elevator for ten minutes and be completely alone. But you can sit with a close friend in silence for those same ten minutes and feel completely together. That invisible thread connecting you and your friend — that sense of real closeness, comfort, and mutual understanding — that is intimacy.

It is a state or quality that exists between people (or sometimes between a person and something else, like a place or an idea). When you say "their intimacy grew over the years," you are describing the depth and quality of their connection, not a single moment or event.

Intimacy has several key ingredients that work together:

Mutual knowledge. Both people know each other at a level deeper than what most people see. You know their fears, their dreams, the things that make them laugh at 2 AM, and the wounds they carry quietly. And they know the same about you.

Trust. Intimacy cannot exist without trust. You are allowing another person to see the real you — the version of yourself that isn't polished for the world. That requires you to believe they won't hurt you, judge you, or walk away because of what they see.

Vulnerability. This is perhaps the most important piece. To be intimate with someone, you have to open up. You have to let your guard down and show parts of yourself that feel private or even scary to reveal. A person who never shows vulnerability can never truly have intimacy, because they are always behind a wall.

Being seen and accepted. True intimacy happens when someone sees all of you — the good parts and the messy, imperfect parts — and accepts you anyway. That feeling of being fully seen and still loved or valued is what makes intimacy so powerful and so rare.

One of the most important things to understand is that intimacy is not only sexual or romantic. This is a very common misunderstanding. Intimacy is a broad idea that takes many shapes:

Emotional intimacy is the most fundamental kind. It is the closeness that comes from sharing your feelings, your inner life, and your personal truths with someone. A best friend who knows about your anxiety, your family troubles, and your secret ambitions shares emotional intimacy with you. This kind can exist in any relationship — friendship, family, romance.

Physical intimacy is closeness through the body. Yes, this includes sexual intimacy — but it also includes a mother holding her child, two friends hugging after a long time apart, or an elderly couple holding hands on a park bench. Physical intimacy is about comfort, warmth, and connection through touch and physical presence. It does not always have a sexual meaning.

Intellectual intimacy is the closeness that forms when two people can share thoughts, ideas, and opinions freely — without fear of being mocked or dismissed. When you can have a deep conversation about ideas you care about, challenge each other's thinking, and feel genuinely understood in your perspective, that is intellectual intimacy.

Experiential intimacy grows from going through life together — sharing meals, trips, hardships, celebrations, and ordinary daily moments. The more you share life with someone, the more intimacy naturally builds, because you become woven into each other's story.

In practice, deep relationships — especially long romantic partnerships or close friendships — tend to have several of these types layered on top of each other, which is why those relationships feel so rich and irreplaceable.

Intimacy is not something that appears all at once. It is built slowly, through repeated acts of trust and vulnerability over time.

It usually starts small. You share something slightly personal. The other person responds with warmth and doesn't misuse what you shared. Because of that, you feel safe enough to share something a little deeper next time. They do the same. Gradually, layer by layer, the closeness grows. This is why people who have been through something difficult together — war, illness, grief — often feel an incredibly strong bond. Shared vulnerability, even in hard circumstances, accelerates intimacy.

The opposite is also true. Intimacy can be broken — through betrayal, dishonesty, cruelty, or emotional distance. When trust is broken, the closeness collapses, because one of its essential foundations has been removed.
Intimacy With Things Other Than People

While intimacy is most commonly used to describe closeness between people, the word is sometimes extended to other contexts:

A small theater with only 80 seats might be called an intimate setting — meaning it feels personal, close, and removed from the large, impersonal world outside. A diary entry might have an intimate tone — meaning it feels personal, raw, and unguarded, as if you are reading someone's private thoughts. A detailed biography might offer intimacy with its subject — meaning it brings you so close to the person's inner life that you feel as though you truly know them.

In all these cases, the core idea remains the same: closeness, depth, and the feeling of something private being shared.

Human beings are wired for connection. Intimacy is what makes relationships feel real and meaningful rather than hollow and surface-level. Without it, even a person surrounded by many people can feel profoundly alone. With it, even a single close relationship can make a person feel anchored, understood, and loved.

This is why intimacy is considered one of the most important human needs — not a luxury, but something fundamental to wellbeing.

Intimacy (noun) = the state or quality of being deeply close to someone, built on mutual trust, vulnerability, and the experience of being truly known and accepted. It is not limited to romance or physical closeness. It is a deep bond between people — or between a person and something — that feels personal, warm, and real in a way that goes far beyond the ordinary.
9153: "Intimate" describes something that is deeply close, deeply personal, or deeply private. The key word in every meaning is depth. Whenever you see "intimate," think: this is not surface-level. This goes deep.

1. A Very Close, Deep Personal Relationship

When "intimate" describes a relationship between people, it means far closer than ordinary friendship. Intimate friends don't just know your name and your job — they know your fears, your secrets, your real feelings. There is genuine trust, warmth, and understanding between them.

  • "She is my most intimate friend." → my deepest, most trusted friend
  • "They share an intimate bond." → a close, private, deeply personal connection

The word signals that two people have let each other in — past the polite outer layer that most people see.

2. Private and Personal (Thoughts, Details, Feelings)

"Intimate" also describes things that are very personal — things you guard carefully and wouldn't share with just anyone.

  • "He revealed intimate details about his past." → private, personal details
  • "She recorded her most intimate thoughts in her diary." → her deepest, most private thoughts

If something is intimate in this sense, sharing it requires trust. It belongs to the inner world of a person, not the public one.

3. Sexual or Romantic Physical Closeness

"Intimate" is frequently used as a polite, formal way of referring to romantic or sexual closeness. It doesn't scream the word "sexual" — it implies it gently. This is one of the most common uses you will encounter.

  • "They became intimate after months of friendship." → they began a romantic/sexual relationship
  • "The film shows an intimate scene between the two leads." → a romantic or sexual scene

Important note: This meaning only activates when the surrounding context is romantic. In a sentence like "an intimate conversation between old friends," there is nothing sexual about it — it just means a deep, private conversation. Context is everything.

4. A Small, Cozy, Private Setting or Atmosphere

When "intimate" describes a place or event, it has nothing to do with people's emotions for each other. Instead, it describes a space that feels small, warm, and private — the opposite of large, cold, and impersonal.

  • "They dined at an intimate little restaurant." → a small, cozy, private-feeling restaurant — not a big, noisy, crowded one
  • "It was an intimate gathering of close friends." → a small, personal gathering, not a large party
  • "The theatre had an intimate atmosphere." → the space was small and warm, making you feel close to the performance

The feeling such a place creates is that you are in your own private world, not surrounded by the noise of the outside. Soft lighting, small tables, quiet voices — these create an intimate setting.

5. Very Deep, Thorough Knowledge of Something

This meaning often surprises learners. "Intimate" can describe knowledge — and when it does, it means you know something so deeply and completely that it feels almost personal, like you have lived inside it.

  • "She has an intimate knowledge of 19th-century French literature." → a deep, thorough, expert-level knowledge
  • "His intimate familiarity with the city made him an ideal guide." → he knows the city from the inside out — not just the tourist spots, but every back street and hidden corner
  • "The book is written with intimate detail about village life." → the author knows this world so deeply the details feel lived-in and real

Surface knowledge is not intimate. Intimate knowledge means you understand something at its deepest level — its patterns, its exceptions, its hidden corners.
The Single Thread Running Through All Five Meanings

Every meaning of "intimate" shares one quality: it goes beyond the surface and reaches something deep, personal, and close. Whether it's a friendship, a secret, a romance, a cozy room, or a field of knowledge — calling it "intimate" always says: this is not shallow. This is deep.

Intimate vs. Close: "Close friends" and "intimate friends" are similar, but "intimate" goes deeper. You can have many close friends. Intimate friendship is rarer and more personal.

Intimate vs. Private: Something "private" is simply not for public viewing. Something "intimate" is private and deeply personal — it carries emotional weight.

Intimate vs. Cozy: A "cozy" room is warm and comfortable. An "intimate" room is all that, plus it creates a feeling of privacy and closeness between the people in it.

Intimate vs. Detailed: "Detailed knowledge" means you know many facts. "Intimate knowledge" means you know something so thoroughly it feels personal — like you've lived with it, not just studied it.

• It does not simply mean "close in physical distance." You wouldn't say "the intimate shop next door."
  • It does not mean "secret" on its own. A secret can be trivial. Something intimate always has personal depth and weight to it.
  • It is not just a synonym for "small." A small stadium is not an intimate one unless it creates that warm, close, private feeling.
A Quick Way to Remember It

Whenever you read or hear "intimate," ask yourself: Does this feel deep, personal, and close — not surface-level? If the answer is yes, you're understanding the word correctly. That single quality of depth and personal closeness is the soul of "intimate" in all its forms.
9154:
To intimate something means to make it known in an indirect, subtle way — to hint at it rather than state it openly and directly.

When you intimate something, you are not announcing it with clear, plain words. You are allowing the other person to understand something through careful suggestion — through a gently chosen phrase, a tone of voice, a meaningful look, or a remark that points toward something without naming it. The message still reaches the listener. They understand what you mean. But you never said it out loud in straightforward language.
A simple example to feel the word:

Imagine a teacher who is reviewing a student's essay. Instead of saying "This essay is not good enough," the teacher says, "I wonder if there's still room to push this piece a little further." The student understands: the essay needs more work. The teacher has intimated that the essay is not yet up to standard, without bluntly saying so.

Another example: A friend is visiting your house, and after a long evening you say, "Well, it's getting quite late, isn't it?" You haven't asked them to leave. But you have intimated that it's time to wrap up.
The most important thing to understand about this word:

The indirectness in "intimate" is deliberate. You are not being vague because you are confused or unsure. You are choosing to communicate sideways rather than head-on. People intimate things for many reasons — because the subject is sensitive or awkward, because bluntness would seem rude in that setting, because they want to protect themselves (after all, you can't be held fully accountable for something you never actually said directly), or simply because the situation calls for a gentler, more delicate touch.
How it differs from similar words (this is important):

"To intimate" sits in a family of words that all involve indirect communication, but each one is slightly different.

To hint is the closest everyday equivalent. "Intimate" is simply the more formal, sophisticated version of "hint." If you say "she hinted," it feels casual. If you say "she intimated," it feels elevated and precise — the kind of word you'd find in a novel or a formal piece of writing.

To imply is about what is embedded within the words you actually use. If you say "The food here used to be better," you imply — without saying — that the food has gotten worse. It's about what your sentence naturally carries inside it. "Intimate" puts more focus on the speaker consciously choosing to communicate something in a delicate, understated way.

To insinuate also means to suggest something indirectly, but it almost always carries a negative or suspicious flavor — you insinuate that someone did something wrong, or has an ulterior motive. "Intimate" is neutral. You can intimate pleasant things, neutral things, or bad things. Insinuate is nearly always used for something unflattering.

To allude means to reference something without naming it directly. "She alluded to her difficult childhood" — she referred to it without going into it fully. With "allude," the focus is on reference and mention. With "intimate," the focus is on actually conveying or communicating something to the listener — making them understand it.
How it is used in real sentences:

"The doctor intimated that the recovery would take longer than first expected." (He suggested it carefully, without giving a direct prognosis.)

"During the meeting, the director intimated that budget cuts were coming." (She didn't announce it officially, but the signal was there.)

"He intimated his disapproval with a long silence and a slow shake of his head." (Sometimes intimating doesn't even require words.)

"The letter intimated that their offer was final and no further negotiations would be entertained." (A formal, written example — the letter's tone made it clear without stating it harshly.)

"Intimate" used as a verb is a formal word. You would not typically use it in casual conversation with friends. You are far more likely to encounter it in literature, journalism, formal speeches, legal contexts, or careful writing. In everyday speech, people simply say "hint" or "suggest." But knowing this word allows you to both understand it when you read it and use it with precision when the moment calls for it.
One common trap — do not confuse it with "intimidate."

These two words look and sound somewhat similar, but they mean entirely different things. To intimidate someone is to make them feel frightened or threatened — to use fear as a form of pressure. To intimate something is to communicate it subtly and indirectly. They are not related in meaning at all. The similarity is only in appearance.
The complete picture in one sentence:
To intimate is to let something be understood — quietly, carefully, and without saying it outright — by leaving just enough of a signal that the thoughtful listener can fill in the rest themselves.
9155:
An intimation is a subtle hint or indirect signal that something exists, is true, or is about to happen — without it being openly or clearly stated.

Think of it this way: when something is announced, it is said loudly and directly. When something is intimated, it is barely whispered — suggested, hinted at, or faintly felt. You often sense an intimation more than you see or hear it clearly.

The single most important quality of an intimation is that it is never direct. It is always a suggestion in the background, never a statement in the foreground.

The word is used in two closely related ways:

1. A hint or indirect suggestion made by a person

This is when someone signals something without saying it outright — through their tone, behaviour, choice of words, or attitude.

"There was an intimation in her voice that she was unhappy with the decision."

She didn't say she was unhappy. But something in her voice quietly suggested it. That quiet suggestion is the intimation.

"He gave no intimation that he was planning to resign."

No hint. No clue. Nothing that pointed toward it.

"The manager's intimation that budget cuts were coming made everyone anxious."

He didn't announce it directly. He hinted at it — and that hint is the intimation.

2. A faint sign or vague feeling that something is happening or coming

This sense is slightly more atmospheric. The "hint" doesn't come from a person's words — it comes from a feeling in the air, a subtle sign in the environment, or an inner sense you can't quite explain.

"There was an intimation of danger as they entered the abandoned building."

Nothing had gone wrong yet. But something — the silence, the darkness, the stillness — suggested that danger was near. That vague sense is the intimation.

"The cold wind carried an intimation of the harsh winter ahead."

The wind didn't announce winter. It only hinted at it.

This second sense often carries a slightly eerie or emotional quality — a feeling just below the surface of awareness. You can't always point to exactly what gave you the intimation, but you feel it.
A Phrase Worth Knowing: "Intimations of Mortality"

You will often encounter the phrase "intimations of mortality" in literature, philosophy, and everyday writing. It means the faint, quiet signals — a grey hair, an aching joint, a friend's illness, a moment of reflection — that remind us, without spelling it out, that life is finite and we will one day die.

These are not loud reminders. They are soft, subtle ones. That softness is precisely why the word intimation is used here, and not announcement or reminder. The word captures something that creeps in quietly rather than arrives loudly.

In some formal and legal contexts — particularly in British and Scottish usage — "intimation" also means a formal official notification or announcement. For example, an "intimation of death" in a formal Scottish context refers to an official notice informing people of someone's passing.

This use is less common in everyday speech today, but you may encounter it in legal documents, official correspondence, or older literature. In this sense, the "indirectness" is gone — it simply means a formal notice. However, unless you are reading legal or formal documents, the word almost always carries the first two senses (hint/indirect signal) in modern usage.

To sharpen your understanding, here is what the word does not mean:

  • It is not a direct statement. If someone says "I am leaving," that is an announcement — not an intimation.
  • It is not a strong or clear indication. If smoke is pouring out of a building, that is a clear sign of fire — not an intimation.
  • It is not a formal command or instruction.

The moment something is said or shown clearly and directly, it stops being an intimation.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Hint — Very similar to intimation, but a hint is often a small, deliberate clue. An intimation can be more unconscious, atmospheric, or emotionally felt — sometimes you can't even point to exactly what gave you the intimation.

Suggestion — A suggestion can be direct ("I suggest we leave"). An intimation is always indirect and understated.

Indication — An indication is a sign that points to something; it can be fairly clear and concrete (a fever is an indication of illness). An intimation is always subtler and vaguer than a clear indication.

Premonition — A premonition is a feeling — usually from within yourself — that something (often bad) is going to happen. An intimation can come from outside you (someone's tone, the atmosphere, a faint sign) or from within. The two words overlap in the emotional sense but are not the same.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

"Intimation" is not a cold, clinical word. It carries a certain quiet seriousness and even a slight sense of unease or gravity. Writers use it when they want to convey that something important is being felt or suggested — but not yet confronted. It is the perfect word for those moments when something significant is in the air but hasn't yet come to the surface.

An intimation is a subtle, indirect hint or signal — something that suggests rather than states, and whispers rather than announces. It can be a hint given by a person through their tone or behaviour, or a faint atmospheric or emotional feeling that something is true or approaching. The rarer formal use means an official notice. The word always points to something sensed at the edges — never something said plainly at the centre.
9156:
To intimidate someone means to make them feel afraid, nervous, or powerless — often on purpose — so that they lose their confidence, feel controlled, or end up doing what you want (or stop doing what they were going to do).

The heart of the word is this: the intimidated person feels smaller and weaker than the intimidator, and that feeling controls their behavior.

1. Deliberate intimidation — using fear as a tool

This is the most common and serious use of the word. Here, someone intentionally tries to frighten another person to get a specific result. The intimidator wants the other person to back down, stay quiet, give up, or obey.

"The gang tried to intimidate the witness into staying silent." "The corrupt official intimidated journalists so they wouldn't publish the story."

Notice the pattern: fear is being used as a weapon. The goal isn't just to scare — it's to control.

2. Unintentional intimidation — feeling overwhelmed or small

Sometimes, a person (or even a situation) can intimidate you without trying to at all. This happens when someone's talent, authority, reputation, or presence makes you feel nervous or inadequate — even though they are not threatening you in any way.

"The professor's vast knowledge intimidated the new student, who was too nervous to ask questions." "She felt intimidated by the long list of job requirements." "The sheer size of the mountain intimidated the beginner hiker."

In these cases, nobody is trying to frighten anyone. The student isn't being threatened. But the feeling is the same — a loss of confidence, a sense of being overpowered. This is why the word fits both situations.

Whether the intimidation is intentional or not, the experience of the person being intimidated is always the same: they feel a rise of fear or nervousness and a loss of freedom to act normally. They might feel too small to speak up, too pressured to push back, or too overwhelmed to move forward. That inner shrinking — that's the signature of being intimidated.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Frighten / Scare — These simply cause sudden fear, often by accident (a loud noise frightens you). Intimidation is different because it makes someone feel overpowered or controlled, not just startled. Intimidation lingers and shapes behavior; fright is often just a moment.

Threaten — To threaten someone is to make an explicit warning of harm: "Do this or else." Intimidation is broader and subtler — you can intimidate someone through your tone, your size, your reputation, or your authority, without ever making a direct threat.

Bully — Bullying is a repeated pattern of intimidation and harm, typically aimed at someone weaker. Intimidation can be a single act. Every bully intimidates, but not every act of intimidation is bullying.

Pressure — Pressuring someone means pushing them to do something, but it doesn't always involve fear. Intimidation always involves a fear or powerlessness element.

Learning how a word behaves in a sentence is as important as knowing its meaning.

Intimidate + someone — "His presence intimidated everyone in the room." (He made them all feel nervous.)

Intimidate + someone + into + [doing something] — "They intimidated her into signing the contract." (They used fear to force her to sign.)

Feel/be intimidated + by — "I felt intimidated by her confidence." (Her confidence made me feel small and nervous.)

Intimidating (adjective) — describes something or someone that causes nervousness or fear. "The interview panel was intimidating."

Intimidated (adjective) — describes the person who feels afraid or overwhelmed as a result. "He walked in feeling intimidated."

Intimidation (noun) — the act itself. "The court condemned the use of intimidation against witnesses."

Intimidator (noun, less common) — a person who intimidates others. "He was a natural intimidator on the sports field."

Intimidation does not require physical danger. You can be intimidated by someone's intelligence, wealth, beauty, social status, or calm authority — none of which are physically threatening. What matters is the imbalance of power, real or imagined, that makes you feel smaller and less free. A nervous student in front of a brilliant teacher, a new employee walking into a boardroom full of executives, a beginner standing at the base of a vast mountain — all of these are genuine examples of intimidation, even without a single threat being made.

That is the full picture of this word: to intimidate is to make someone feel too small to act freely, whether through deliberate fear or simply through overwhelming presence.
9157:
When you are intimidated, you feel a mix of fear, nervousness, and self-doubt — not because something is physically dangerous, but because something or someone makes you feel smaller, less capable, or overpowered compared to them.

It is the feeling of looking at something and thinking: "This is bigger than me. I'm not sure I can handle this. I don't feel good enough here."
What Makes It Different from Just "Scared"

This is the most important distinction to understand.

Scared is about danger — you're afraid of getting hurt. A dog growling at you makes you scared.

Intimidated is about a power gap — you feel outmatched, outclassed, or overwhelmed. You're not necessarily in danger. You just feel like the other person, thing, or situation is far above your level, and that makes you shrink.

For example:

  • Walking into a room full of world-class experts when you're a beginner → you feel intimidated, not scared.
  • Being chased by someone → you feel scared.

Sometimes both feelings can mix together, but the heart of "intimidated" is always that sense of "I am not enough for this."

You can feel intimidated by many different things:

A person — Someone who is very powerful, very skilled, very authoritative, or very aggressive can make you feel intimidated. A strict teacher, a famous expert, a confident boss, or even someone who speaks very aggressively can trigger this feeling. Their presence alone makes you feel unsure of yourself.

A situation — Walking into a big job interview, speaking in front of a large audience, or entering a very competitive environment for the first time can be intimidating.

A task — Looking at a very difficult exam, a massive project, or a skill that seems impossibly hard can make you feel intimidated.

Size or scale — Even something non-human, like standing at the base of a huge mountain or walking into a grand, enormous building, can make a person feel intimidated — because the sheer scale makes you feel tiny and powerless.

The common thread in all of these: there is something that seems far greater than you, and your mind reacts by making you feel small and unsure.
How It Feels on the Inside

When you are intimidated, several things happen in your mind and body at the same time:

  • You lose confidence, even if you were confident before.
  • You start doubting yourself: "Can I really do this? Am I good enough?"
  • You feel a kind of pressure or tension in your chest.
  • Your mind may go blank when you try to speak or act.
  • You may feel like you don't belong in that place or situation.
  • Your heart might beat faster, your hands might feel slightly shaky.

It is an uncomfortable, shrinking feeling — as if the situation or person is pressing down on you and making you feel less capable than you actually are.

Intimidation doesn't just stay inside — it changes how people act:

  • They go quiet when they would normally speak up.
  • They hesitate before doing something, or avoid it entirely.
  • They become overly careful or awkward in their movements and words.
  • They stop expressing their real opinions, because they worry about being judged.
  • They may back away from a challenge, even if they are actually capable of it.

This is why feeling intimidated can be harmful — it can stop you from doing things you are perfectly capable of doing, simply because your confidence has been crushed by comparison.

Like most feelings, intimidation comes in different strengths:

Slightly intimidated — A small knot of nervousness. You feel a little unsure, but you can still function normally. Example: meeting a slightly more experienced colleague for the first time.

Moderately intimidated — You feel noticeably unsure of yourself. You may go quieter than usual, choose your words more carefully, or hold back from participating fully.

Deeply / completely intimidated — You feel almost frozen. Your confidence nearly disappears. You might struggle to speak, think clearly, or act at all. Example: a very shy student being asked to present in front of a national television audience.
How the Word Is Used Grammatically

"Intimidated" is an adjective — it describes the state or condition of a person.

Most commonly, it follows a verb like "feel," "look," "seem," or "be":

  • She felt intimidated.
  • He looked intimidated.
  • They seemed intimidated.
  • I was completely intimidated.

Almost always, it is followed by the word "by" to tell us what caused the feeling:

  • She felt intimidated by his loud, confident voice.
  • He was intimidated by the complexity of the question.

Less commonly, it sits directly before a noun:

  • The intimidated student sat silently in the corner.

Reading a wide range of sentences is one of the best ways to make a word stick in your memory:

In a professional setting:

  • She was intimidated by her new manager, who had 30 years of experience in the field.
  • He felt intimidated walking into the office on his first day — everyone seemed so polished and confident.

In an academic setting:

  • The young student was intimidated by the thickness of the textbook.
  • Don't feel intimidated by difficult questions — just take them one step at a time.

In a social setting:

  • I felt intimidated at the party because everyone else seemed to know each other.
  • She was so charming and well-spoken that many people found her intimidating — they felt intimidated just talking to her.

In a competitive setting:

  • The young chess player felt intimidated sitting across from the national champion.
  • The new team was completely intimidated by their opponents' reputation.

In a physical setting:

  • Standing at the edge of the cliff, he felt intimidated by the sheer drop below.
  • The enormous crowd in the stadium made the performers feel intimidated before they even stepped on stage.

In an everyday setting:

  • I've always been a little intimidated by cooking elaborate meals — there are so many steps.
  • She was intimidated by the long list of requirements on the job application.

Here is something that makes this word truly click:

Being intimidated is often not based on reality. Many people feel intimidated by things they are actually capable of handling — but the feeling of being outmatched is so strong that it overrides their rational confidence. This is why people often say things like "Don't be intimidated — you're more ready for this than you think."

In other words, the feeling of being intimidated is real and powerful, but the reason for it is often an illusion — your mind exaggerating the gap between you and the challenge in front of you.
One-Line Summary to Anchor It All
Intimidated = feeling nervous, unsure, and small because something or someone seems far more powerful, skilled, or overwhelming than you — leading you to doubt yourself and hold back.
9158:
Something is intimidating if it makes you feel nervous, small, or unsure of yourself — because it seems too powerful, too difficult, too impressive, or too threatening for you to easily face or handle.

When something intimidates you, your confidence drops. You feel like hesitating, backing away, or doubting whether you're capable enough.
The Two Main Ways Something Can Be Intimidating

1. It feels threatening or dangerous.
A barking dog blocking your path is intimidating. An aggressive person who looks ready to fight is intimidating. This triggers a fear response — you feel unsafe.

2. It feels too impressive, too big, or too far beyond you.
This is the more common, everyday use. A 1,000-page textbook on your first day of study is intimidating. A world-class chess grandmaster sitting across from you is intimidating. You don't feel scared in a dangerous sense — you feel small, inadequate, or out of your depth.

Both types share the same result: they shake your confidence and make you feel hesitant or overwhelmed.
Who or What Can Be Intimidating?

Almost anything:

  • A person: "My new boss has an intimidating personality — she never smiles and always looks serious."
  • A task: "Learning to code felt intimidating at first."
  • A place: "Walking into a grand courtroom for the first time can be intimidating."
  • A situation: "Speaking in front of 500 people is intimidating for most people."
  • A subject: "Quantum physics seems intimidating, but the basics are learnable."
  • A scale or size: "The sheer length of this novel is intimidating."
Intentional vs. Unintentional — A Key Nuance

A person can be intimidating without meaning to be.

A very tall, quiet, serious person may intimidate others simply by their presence — they never intended to. A highly skilled expert can make beginners feel intimidated just by how effortlessly they perform.

But a person can also deliberately try to be intimidating — by staring you down, speaking aggressively, or using their authority to make you feel powerless.

The word "intimidating" can describe both situations. You rely on context to know which is meant.
Is "Intimidating" Always Negative?

Not always — but it almost always signals that someone feels less confident in response to it.

Sometimes it's used with a neutral or even admiring tone:

  • "She has an intimidating level of talent." (You're in awe — humbled, not scared.)
  • "The mountain's intimidating scale drew climbers from around the world."

But in most everyday use, calling something intimidating means it's making someone feel anxious or hesitant — which is a negative experience for that person, even if the thing itself is neutral or good.
It's Partly Subjective

The same thing can be intimidating to one person and perfectly normal to another.

  • A loud, crowded city might be intimidating to someone from a quiet village, but not to a city-dweller.
  • A difficult math problem might be intimidating to a student but exciting to a mathematician.

So "intimidating" describes a relationship between something and a person's response to it — not a fixed quality of the thing itself. The thing doesn't change; it's your perception and confidence level that determines whether it feels intimidating.
Example Sentences

1. "The interview panel was so intimidating that he forgot everything he'd prepared."
  2. "Don't let her intimidating appearance fool you — she's actually very warm."
  3. "The mountain looked intimidating from the base, but the hike wasn't actually that hard."
  4. "Learning a new language can feel intimidating, but it gets easier with time."
  5. "He had an intimidating stare that made people uncomfortable."
  6. "The sheer amount of work ahead of us was intimidating."
  7. "She walked into the room with an intimidating confidence — everyone fell silent."

Notice how in sentence 7, "intimidating confidence" is almost a compliment — it means her confidence was so strong that it made others feel a little unsure of themselves.
Words Closely Related to "Intimidating"

Understanding these will show you exactly where "intimidating" fits among similar words:

Daunting — Makes a task feel too big to even begin. Very close to "intimidating" but used almost exclusively for tasks and challenges, rarely for people. "The project is daunting" = I don't know where to start. "Intimidating" works for both people and tasks; "daunting" mainly for tasks.

Formidable — Inspires fear or deep respect because of power, strength, or ability. Slightly more formal and stronger. A "formidable opponent" is one you genuinely fear facing. Something formidable commands respect almost by right; something intimidating just makes you personally feel small.

Frightening — Causes actual fear. Clearly stronger than "intimidating." A frightening movie makes your heart pound; an intimidating boss just makes you nervous before a meeting.

Overwhelming — So much in quantity or intensity that you can't cope. An overwhelming workload might not be intimidating (it doesn't necessarily shake your confidence) — it's just too much to handle. "Overwhelming" is about quantity and overload; "intimidating" is about confidence and power.

Imposing — Grand and impressive in size or appearance, demanding attention and respect. An imposing building is large, serious, and commands your notice. "Imposing" is more about the visual presence of something; "intimidating" is about the emotional effect it has on you.

Threatening — Signals that something could cause you harm. More directly about danger than "intimidating." All threatening things are intimidating, but not all intimidating things are threatening — a genius professor is intimidating but not threatening.
The Opposite of "Intimidating"

Depending on context, the opposite might be:

  • Approachable (for a person — easy to talk to, not scary)
  • Welcoming (for a place or person)
  • Manageable (for a task — feels doable, within reach)
  • Reassuring (for a situation — makes you feel calm and capable)
  • Encouraging (for feedback or an environment)
The Word Family

Since you'll encounter these related forms:

  • To intimidate (verb) = to deliberately make someone feel afraid or unsure, usually to control them or gain power over them. "He tried to intimidate the witness into staying silent."
  • Intimidating (adjective) = describes something that has the quality of causing this feeling. This is what you asked about.
  • Intimidated (adjective) = describes the person who is on the receiving end of this feeling. "She felt intimidated by the crowd." Note: you describe a thing as intimidating, but a person as intimidated.
  • Intimidation (noun) = the act or the experience itself. "The defendant claimed it was an act of intimidation."

A simple test to remember which to use: if you're describing the source of the feeling, use "intimidating." If you're describing the person experiencing the feeling, use "intimidated."

"The exam was intimidating." (The exam is the source.)
"I felt intimidated by the exam." (You are the one experiencing it.)
The Complete Picture

To summarize everything cleanly:

Something is intimidating when it makes you feel nervous, small, hesitant, or out of your depth — whether because it's powerful, difficult, impressive, or threatening. It doesn't have to be dangerous to be intimidating; it just has to make you feel like you might not be enough to handle it. The word applies to people, tasks, places, situations, and ideas. Whether something feels intimidating is partly personal — it depends on who you are and what you're used to. And the thing causing the feeling may or may not be doing so intentionally.
9159:
Intimidation is the act of making someone feel frightened or threatened in order to influence what they do or don't do. It is the process of using fear as a tool of control.

When intimidation happens, one person (or group) creates a sense of danger, threat, or overwhelming pressure in another person's mind — and that fear pushes the other person to obey, back down, stay silent, or act in a way they otherwise wouldn't choose to freely.

Think of it this way: intimidation is fear used as a weapon of influence.
Breaking It Down: The Three Core Parts

Every act of intimidation has three parts working together.

The intimidator is the person (or group) doing the intimidating. They hold — or appear to hold — some form of power, whether physical, social, emotional, or situational.

The target is the person being intimidated. They feel threatened, unsafe, or overwhelmed, and this feeling shapes their choices.

The goal is the outcome the intimidator wants — getting the target to do something, stop doing something, or stay silent about something.

Without all three elements, it's not quite intimidation. It's just fear in general.

Intimidation doesn't always require a direct threat. It works by making a person feel that something bad will happen to them — or to someone they care about — if they don't comply. That feeling of danger doesn't even have to be based in reality. As long as the target believes the threat is real, the intimidation is working.

This is important: intimidation operates in the mind of the target. The intimidator plants a seed of fear, and that fear does the rest of the work.
The Many Forms Intimidation Can Take

Intimidation is not a single, fixed action. It wears many costumes.

Physical intimidation uses the body or the threat of physical harm. Someone standing over you, blocking your path, showing a weapon, or using sheer physical size to make you feel small or unsafe — this is physical intimidation.

Verbal intimidation uses words. Shouting, making direct threats ("if you tell anyone, you'll regret it"), issuing ultimatums, or using a tone of voice designed to frighten — all of this counts.

Psychological or emotional intimidation is more subtle but often the most powerful. It involves tactics like making someone constantly doubt themselves, reminding someone of what you could do to them, using guilt or shame as weapons, making someone feel watched, or destroying their sense of safety over time. Emotional abusers are often masters of this form.

Social intimidation uses status, reputation, or group power. A popular person threatening to humiliate someone publicly, a boss hinting that your job is at risk, a gang using their collective reputation to silence a witness — these are all social forms of intimidation.

Silent or implied intimidation involves no words at all. A cold, prolonged stare. Following someone. Standing too close. Showing up somewhere uninvited. These actions communicate a threat without stating one openly, and they are no less real.

Most of the time, intimidation is deliberate — the intimidator knows exactly what they are doing and wants the target to feel afraid. They are consciously using fear to get what they want.

However, intimidation can also be unintentional. A very tall, physically imposing person might intimidate others without trying to. A person with great authority — a judge, a strict teacher, a powerful boss — might make others feel too afraid to speak freely, even when they have no intention of threatening anyone. In this case, the effect of intimidation is real even though the intent isn't there.

This distinction matters because the experience of the person being intimidated is real regardless of intention.

Intimidation vs. Fear: Fear is a feeling that can arise from anything — a thunderstorm, a horror movie, an accident. Intimidation specifically involves another person or group deliberately (or at least effectively) causing that fear to control behavior. Intimidation always has a social dimension; fear does not.

Intimidation vs. A Threat: A threat is a specific statement or action that says "something bad will happen if you don't comply." A threat is one method of intimidation, but intimidation is the broader process. You can intimidate someone without ever making an explicit threat — just your presence, your reputation, or your past behavior can be enough.

Intimidation vs. Persuasion: Persuasion tries to change someone's mind using reason, evidence, or appeal. Intimidation bypasses the mind entirely and goes straight for the emotions — specifically fear. Persuasion respects a person's freedom to decide; intimidation hijacks it.

Intimidation vs. Coercion: These are closely related. Coercion is forcing someone to act against their will through pressure or threats. Intimidation is often the tool used to coerce — you intimidate someone in order to coerce them. Think of intimidation as the psychological weapon and coercion as the outcome it produces.

Intimidation shows up in ordinary life more than people realize.

In relationships, an abusive partner may use intimidation to stop the other person from leaving, speaking to friends, or reporting abuse. In a school, a bully intimidates classmates to make them hand over lunch money or stay silent. In a workplace, a domineering manager may intimidate employees into working unpaid overtime by making them fear for their jobs. In politics, authoritarian governments use intimidation against journalists, activists, and voters to suppress opposition.

Even in sports and competition, intimidation is used — a basketball player staring down an opponent, an MMA fighter using their reputation to mentally weaken a challenger before a fight even begins. Here it is usually considered a legitimate psychological tactic rather than something harmful.

In law, intimidation takes on a very specific and serious meaning. It refers to the criminal act of using threats or fear to prevent someone from exercising their legal rights.

Examples of illegal intimidation include: threatening a witness to stop them from testifying in court (called witness intimidation), threatening voters to influence their vote or stop them from voting (voter intimidation), or threatening a juror to influence their verdict (jury intimidation).

In most legal systems around the world, intimidation of this kind is a criminal offense on its own — separate from whatever underlying crime is being committed. The law treats it seriously because it directly attacks the ability of people to seek justice and exercise their rights freely.

Since you're learning, it helps to know the related forms of this word:

Intimidate is the verb — the action. "He tried to intimidate her into silence."

Intimidation is the noun — the act or process itself. "The intimidation she faced stopped her from speaking up."

Intimidating is the adjective that describes something or someone that causes fear or makes you feel small. "The boss had an intimidating presence."

Intimidated is the adjective that describes how the target feels. "She felt intimidated by the crowd."

Intimidator is the noun for the person who does it. "The intimidator used his size to threaten others."

Intimidation is about power and control through fear. It is one of the oldest human tools for dominating others — and also one of the most psychologically damaging when used in harmful ways. Understanding it helps you recognize it when it happens to you, name it clearly, and respond to it with awareness rather than just reacting with blind fear.

Whenever you see someone using another person's fear to dictate their choices — whether in a conversation, a relationship, a courtroom, or a political arena — you are watching intimidation at work.
